description_full: Nucor Corporation engages in the manufacture and sale of steel and steel products. The company operates in three segments: Steel Mills, Steel Products, and Raw Materials. The Steel Mills segment produces hot-rolled, cold-rolled, and galvanized sheet steel products; plate steel products; wide-flange beams, beam blanks, and H-piling and sheet piling structural steel products; and bar steel products, such as blooms, billets, concrete reinforcing and merchant bars, and engineered special bar quality products. This segment sells its products to steel service centers, fabricators, and manufacturers in the United States, Canada, and Mexico, as well as engages in the steel trading and rebar distribution businesses. The Steel Products segment offers steel joists and joist girders, steel decks, and galvanized torque tubes for use in solar arrays, hollow structural section steel tubing, electrical conduit, fabricated concrete reinforcing steel, cold finished steel, steel fasteners, steel grating and expanded metal, wire and wire mesh, metal building systems, insulated metal panels, steel racking, overhead doors, and utility towers and structures for communications and energy transmission. This segment is also involved in the piling distribution business. The Raw Materials segment produces direct reduced iron (DRI); brokers ferrous and nonferrous metals, pig iron, hot briquetted iron, and DRI; supplies ferro-alloys; processes ferrous and nonferrous scrap metal; and engages in the natural gas production and industrial gas business. This segment sells its ferrous scrap to electric arc furnace steel mills and foundries for manufacturing process; and nonferrous scrap metal to aluminum can producers, secondary aluminum smelters, steel mills and other processors, and consumers of various nonferrous metals. Nucor Corporation was founded in 1905 and is based in Charlotte, North Carolina.

financial_summary: Nucor Corporation is a large-cap basic materials business with a $55.6B market cap on $32.5B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -8% over the past three years and +7% annually across the full decade, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome.
Returns on capital run at 24% against a 10% cost of capital — a 14-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat.
The company is burning through $188M of cash, and without positive owner earnings any valuation rests on hope rather than evidence.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.2× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage of 15× is fortress-like.

Shareholder yield of 2.2% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sector_headwinds.text: Price sits 44% above estimated fair value — no margin of safety left, and the cushion against estimate error has been bid away (confirmed by 1 other valuation measure)
Fragmented industry with below-average profit capture — no moat to protect margins
Volatile returns on capital suggest the moat is narrower than a snapshot ROIC implies
Insiders are net sellers (100% sell ratio, net $38.1M) — the people closest to the business are reducing their personal stake
Cyclical sectors like Basic Materials tend to underperform in slowdowns
Late-cycle dynamics increase the probability of a slowdown
Commodity price volatility and cost-curve position — in a downturn only the lowest-cost producer has a business, and the rest carry the overhead.
Environmental remediation liability — tightening regulations on emissions, tailings, and water use create open-ended balance-sheet risk that grows with each legislative cycle.
Trade policy and tariff whiplash — materials producers are first-order casualties of protectionist swings, and margin gets squeezed from both input and output pricing.

sector_tailwinds: Reinvestment rate supports 24% organic growth capacity — capital is compounding inside the business
Altman Z comfortably in the safe zone — a fortress balance sheet on this measure
42 consecutive years of dividend payments — an operating record that makes the dividend claim credible
Healthy payout ratio leaves room for both dividend growth and reinvestment
ROIC sits in the top quartile of Basic Materials peers — the moat is wider than the neighbourhood

sect: Its 8% operating margin is roughly in line with the Basic Materials median (10%).
It earns less of the sector's profit than its revenue share would suggest (0.60x).
It accounts for 1.9% of sector revenue and 1.2% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+13.7% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.04 across 219 companies in the universe; the top four hold 25% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 76% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 9% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 15% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 32% and a beta of 1.18, it moves roughly with the market.
Liquidity is deep, with about $300.9M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 48% in the 2020 crash, 41% in the 2022 bear market and 68% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $170 (margin of safety -44%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 54%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $136 to $218 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 221% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of -0.3% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 4.3% (vs the 8% bar).
The 16 covering analysts target $296 on average, 21% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
The price implies 12.8% annual cash-flow growth, 6pp more than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 24% clears the cost of capital of 9.8% by 14pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.89).
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.85x.
ROE of 8% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.7x equity multiplier).
It spends 0.4% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 1.2x net debt to EBITDA ($2.7B of cash against $7.1B of debt), with interest covered 15.1x.
growth: Revenue has compounded at -7.8% over 3 years, 10.0% over 5 years and 7.1% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 25%).
At current returns, reinvesting 100% of profits supports about 24.0% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Capex runs 2.8x depreciation (10.5% of sales), so it is building capacity for future growth.
Its Rule of 40 score is 9, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 4.2% on average.
own: Insiders own a modest 1.2%, and institutions hold 81%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (25 sales, net $38.1M sold).
It returns 2.2% a year to shareholders (1.3% in buybacks and 0.9% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 4.5% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 42 consecutive years, raising it 0.8% a year over the last five.
people: With about 33,000 employees, each generates about $985K of revenue, 1.5x the Basic Materials median, and productivity has risen 6.9% a year.
Free cash flow is negative, at -$6K per employee.
CEO pay is $4.1M (4x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (2/10, lower is better).
